headline: New Hampshire drought lingers despite nor’easter rain
dek: The latest U.S. Drought Monitor update says 96.05% of the state remains abnormally dry, with more than half in moderate drought after the weekend storm.
body: A weekend nor’easter delivered at least an inch of rain to most of New Hampshire, but it did little to change the state’s drought picture. As of Oct. 1, 96.05% of New Hampshire was at least abnormally dry and 53.33% was in moderate drought, according to the latest update summarized by [WMUR](https://www.wmur.com/article/new-hampshire-drought-noreaster-report-101/73982475). The figures describe the share of the state’s land area in each category, not the percentage of residents or individual properties affected.

The limited change matters because a single storm can improve surface moisture without repairing longer-term deficits in streams, reservoirs, groundwater and soils. WMUR reported that the rainfall brought few gains to northern New England, while wetter conditions farther south improved portions of Connecticut, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. Maine and New Hampshire remained broadly dry, although Maine’s conditions were more severe in the report’s regional comparison.

The U.S. Drought Monitor classifies abnormally dry conditions as D0. D0 is not technically drought, but it can describe a landscape that is unusually dry or recovering from drought. Moderate drought is D1, the first formal drought category. The Monitor says D1 can bring some damage to crops and pastures, higher fire risk, low streams, reservoirs or wells, and developing or imminent water shortages in some places. Those are broad indicators; they do not mean every New Hampshire community or household is experiencing the same conditions. More information is available through the [U.S. Drought Monitor’s current map and data tools](https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/).

The latest statewide percentages also mask a sharp geographic contrast. WMUR reported that just under 4% of New Hampshire had no drought conditions, concentrated in a small area in southwestern Hillsborough County and part of Cheshire County. In other words, a resident may see a different situation depending on the watershed, soil, elevation and water source serving a particular town. The statewide map is useful for tracking the regional pattern, but local water managers and emergency officials are the authorities for specific restrictions or well concerns.

New Hampshire’s current conditions are nevertheless better than they were at this point last year. WMUR reported that nearly the entire state had been in severe or extreme drought in late September 2025, with central New Hampshire among the hardest-hit areas. The comparison shows why the current report should be read as a measure of ongoing stress rather than a declaration that the state is facing the same level of crisis as last fall.

The U.S. Drought Monitor is updated weekly from a combination of precipitation, soil-moisture, streamflow, groundwater and other indicators. Its maps are released on Thursdays after a Tuesday morning data cutoff, so the Oct. 1 assessment captures conditions through the latest reporting cycle rather than every hour of rainfall. That timing also means a future wet period could change the map, while a short burst of rain may not be enough to move deeper hydrologic measures.

For residents, the next developments to watch are not just the next rain total but whether water levels recover across the systems that supply farms, forests, fire departments and homes. People who rely on private wells should use their town or state notices for local guidance instead of treating a statewide percentage as a diagnosis of their own supply. The immediate message from the latest report is narrower: the nor’easter offered some rain, but it did not end New Hampshire’s dry spell, and more sustained moisture will be needed for a broader recovery.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New Hampshire drought persists after weekend nor’easter
seoDescription: New Hampshire remains broadly abnormally dry, with 53.33% of the state in moderate drought after the weekend nor’easter.
